tierWindow.goal: Understand what reflection is and why it matters, and recognise it as a deliberate, honest habit of looking back that drives your development as a learner.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Recognition, recall, description and guided application (understand and identify).
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Well-defined, one idea at a time; a single simple model; settled distinctions such as reflection vs description.
tierWindow.autonomy: High scaffolding; worked examples; feedback confirms and explains; frequent low-stakes checks.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: No prior experience of treating reflection as a deliberate practice is assumed. The learner is early in their studies and may have been asked to 'reflect' on a task without a clear sense of what that means or how it differs from simply describing what happened; teach from first principles.

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, what reflection is and why it matters. Second, a simple model for reflecting: describe, reflect, take action. Third, how to keep a reflection honest and balanced. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about reflection: what it means to reflect at university, and how to do it. By the end you will be able to explain what reflection is and why it matters, describe a simple model for reflecting, and recognise what keeps a reflection honest and balanced.

Reflection is not an add-on. 'Reflect on your learning' is one of the most common things you will be asked to do, in coursework, on placements, and in professional life. Knowing what it really involves, and having a model and the honesty to use it, turns a vague instruction into a habit that drives your development.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain what reflection is and why it matters, describe a simple reflective model, identify what makes reflection honest and balanced.

practiceConnection.academic: Reflection is the habit that turns experience into learning. Every assignment you review, every placement or project you look back on, every time you ask why something went as it did, draws on the same skill. Build it now and it carries into every module of your degree, and into the professional practice that expects you to keep learning from what you do.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced reflective practice courses take reflection into structured cycles, turning it into sustained action and into a professional practice you own. Going wider: the same habit underpins Understanding Learning, Assessment and Feedback, Academic Writing, and Work-Based and Experiential Learning, where you put reflection to work on real tasks.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Reflection is no longer a vague instruction: it is something you can describe and begin to do. You can explain what reflection is - a deliberate, honest look back that helps you learn - and why it matters for your development. You have a simple model to follow: describe, reflect, take action. And you know what keeps a reflection honest and balanced: looking at the positives first, never landing all on one side, and being truthful without being harsh. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, reflection is something you practise across your studies and beyond. Each piece of work you review, each placement or project you look back on, each honest account of what you would change, is the habit at work. It is also what professional life expects: the ability to learn from experience, deliberately and honestly, travels well beyond your degree.
